definition: A statement that is either true or false, such as 2 + 3 = 4 (which is false).
A statement with variables, like "p is prime". It becomes a proposition once the variables get values.
"If A then B." It is false only when A is true and B is false, so false implies anything.
NOT B → NOT A. It always means the same thing as A → B, unlike the converse B → A.
A ⊆ B means every element of A is also in B. The empty set is a subset of every set.
A proposition we agree to assume true as a starting point for proofs, declared up front.
A valid way to get a new true statement from known ones. For example, P and P → Q together give Q.
To prove P → Q, assume NOT Q and show NOT P. It works because the two statements are equivalent.
Assume the claim is false, then derive something both true and false. So the claim must be true.
The first instance of an induction, such as P(0), proved directly. It starts the chain.
A proof that, for an arbitrary n, P(n) implies P(n + 1).
If P(0) holds and P(n) → P(n + 1) for every n, then P(n) holds for every natural number n.
A statement that is always true, whatever its parts are. Example: C OR NOT C.
Prove the claim separately under each case of a split, then show the cases cover every possibility.
Cases that together cover every possible situation. Forgetting one breaks the whole proof.
6: the fewest people that guarantees 3 mutual friends or 3 mutual strangers. Five people are not enough.
To prove P(n), you may assume P(k) for every k less than n. It is just as valid as ordinary induction.
A line-up of tournament teams in which each team beat the next. One always exists in a round robin.
A model of a process: a set of states, a start state, and the transitions allowed between states.
A state that some execution, starting from the start state and following legal transitions, ends at.
A true/false property of states that every transition keeps true: if it holds before a move, it holds after.
A predicate true in every reachable state. Proved by showing it holds at the start and is preserved.
Two items in the wrong relative order: the larger one comes first. The 8-puzzle keeps their count's parity fixed.
A number computed from each state. If it is a natural number that drops every step, the machine must stop.
An expression with a fixed number of operations, no dots or sigma, that a calculator can evaluate directly.
1 + x + x² + … + xⁿ⁻¹, which equals (1 − xⁿ)/(1 − x) when x ≠ 1.
Change a sum slightly, such as multiplying by x or reversing it, then combine with the original so most terms cancel.
An educated guess at a formula's shape with unknown constants, solved from small cases, then proved by induction.
Rewriting a double sum so the inner and outer indices trade places, covering exactly the same pairs.
Bound a sum by the integral I of its function: I plus the smaller end term ≤ sum ≤ I plus the larger end term.
Hₙ = 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n. No closed form, but Hₙ ~ ln n, so it grows without bound, very slowly.
f ~ g means f(n)/g(n) tends to 1: the functions agree except for lower-order terms.
f ∈ O(g) if some constant C and start n₀ give f(n) ≤ C·g(n) for every n ≥ n₀.
f ∈ Θ(g) means f ∈ O(g) and g ∈ O(f): the same growth rate up to constant factors.
f ∈ o(g) means f(n)/g(n) tends to 0. A lower-order term is exactly a little-o term.
n! ~ √(2πn)·(n/e)ⁿ. Very accurate: within 1% already at n = 10.
A sequence where each term is defined from earlier terms, such as T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1.
A direct formula for the n-th term, so you do not need to compute all earlier terms first.
Spot a pattern in the first few terms, guess a formula, then prove the guess by induction.
Substitute a recurrence into itself repeatedly, keeping levels separate, until a pattern appears.
Split the input into smaller parts, solve each part recursively, then combine the answers. Merge sort is the classic example.
Gives a Theta bound for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) by comparing root work f(n) with the n^(log_b a) leaves.
a divides b when b = k·a for some integer k. Every integer divides 0.
A number s·a + t·b where s and t are integers, possibly negative.
The largest integer that divides both numbers; gcd(0, 0) is defined as 0.
For integer n and positive d, there are unique q and r with n = q·d + r and 0 ≤ r < d.
Repeatedly replace (x, y) with (y, x rem y) until y = 0; then x is the GCD. Takes logarithmically many steps.
The extended Euclidean algorithm: finds gcd(a, b) along with integers s, t such that gcd(a, b) = s·a + t·b.
a ≡ b (mod n) when n divides a − b; equivalently, a and b leave the same remainder when divided by n.
The remainder of a divided by n, always between 0 and n − 1. Python's a % n matches it for positive n.
All integers sharing one remainder mod n, such as {…, −4, 1, 6, 11, …} mod 5.
A number a⁻¹ with a·a⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod n). It exists exactly when gcd(a, n) = 1, and the Pulverizer finds it.
Two integers whose greatest common divisor is 1, such as 7 and 30.
If p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p), so exponents shrink mod p − 1.
Shift every letter by a secret k mod 26. Only 26 keys exist, so trying them all breaks it instantly.
Breaking a substitution cipher by matching the most common ciphertext symbols to common letters like E and T.
Anyone encrypts with a published key; only the owner decrypts with a separate secret key. No prior meeting is needed.
Public key (n, e) with n = pq. Secret key (n, d), where d is the inverse of e mod (p−1)(q−1).
Finding d requires (p−1)(q−1), which would let you factor n, and nobody knows a fast way to factor huge numbers.
If p and q are coprime, knowing x mod p and x mod q determines x uniquely mod pq.
A nonempty set of vertices plus a set of edges, each joining two different vertices. No loops and no repeated edges.
The number of edges touching a vertex.
The sum of all vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges, because every edge has two endpoints.
Vertices split into two sides L and R, and every edge has one endpoint on each side.
The fewest colors needed so that no edge joins two vertices of the same color.
Color vertices in a fixed order, each taking the smallest color its colored neighbors don't use. Max degree d means at most d + 1 colors.
A set of edges where no two share an endpoint, so everyone has at most one partner.
Maximal: no edge can be added. Maximum: no larger matching exists anywhere. Maximal does not imply maximum.
A matching covering every vertex. In a bipartite graph this requires both sides to be the same size.
Two people not matched together who each prefer the other to their assigned partner.
Unheld applicants propose down their lists; evaluators hold their favourite and reject the rest. Stops when a day has no rejections; always stable.
Gale-Shapley gives every proposer their best feasible partner and every evaluator their worst feasible partner, simultaneously.
A sequence of vertices joined by edges, repeats allowed. Its length is the number of edges.
A walk that never repeats a vertex or an edge. Any shortest walk is a path.
A largest group of vertices that can all reach each other. Every vertex belongs to exactly one.
A closed walk using every edge exactly once. It exists exactly when the graph is connected and all degrees are even.
A connected graph with no cycles. A tree with n vertices always has n − 1 edges.
A vertex of degree 1. Every tree with 2 or more vertices has at least two, and pruning one leaves a tree.
A graph whose edges are arrows (ordered pairs). Loops and opposite pairs of arrows are allowed.
A largest set of vertices that can all reach each other along the arrows.
A directed acyclic graph: a digraph with no cycles. It models tasks with precedence constraints.
A listing of all vertices where each one comes before everything it can reach. Every DAG has one.
A source has no incoming arrows and a sink has no outgoing arrows. Every DAG has at least one of each.
A set of vertices where none can reach another. These tasks can safely run at the same time.
A domain, a codomain, and a set of pairs saying which elements are related. Picture it as arrows from left to right.
A relation with exactly one arrow out of every input and exactly one arrow into every output. It proves two sets have equal size.
A relation where every input has exactly one output. This is what mathematicians usually mean by function.
Reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. It captures sameness and splits a set into disjoint blocks.
Reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive, like ≤, ⊆, or divides. Some pairs may be incomparable.
Multiply the counts when you make one choice AND another. Add the counts for disjoint options, one OR another.
If step i of a sequence of choices always has n_i options, whatever came before, the total is n_1 × n_2 × ... × n_k.
A function where every element of the target set is hit by exactly k elements of the source set.
If a map from A to B is k-to-1, then the size of B equals the size of A divided by k.
C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n − k)!): the number of ways to pick a k-element subset from n items, order ignored.
Another name for n choose k. The name comes from the binomial theorem, where these numbers are the coefficients.
A step-by-step way to build objects. It counts correctly only if it builds every object in the set exactly once.
To count a union, add the set sizes, subtract pairwise overlaps, add triple overlaps, and so on with alternating signs.
If more items than boxes are each put in a box, some box must hold at least two items.
If there are more than k times as many items as boxes, some box holds at least k + 1 items.
Proving two expressions are equal by showing both count the same set in different ways. Also called double counting.
C(n, k) = C(n−1, k−1) + C(n−1, k): each Pascal's triangle entry is the sum of the two above it.
(x + y)^n = Σ C(n, k) x^k y^(n−k). The coefficient counts ways to pick which k factors contribute x.
The set of all possible outcomes of a random process. In this course it is nonempty and countable.
One complete way a random process can turn out. In a tree diagram, it is one root-to-leaf path.
A function Pr assigning each outcome a number between 0 and 1, with all values adding up to 1.
Any set of outcomes. Its probability is the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes it contains.
Find outcomes with a tree, label edges with probabilities, multiply along paths, choose the event, then add.
A space where every outcome is equally likely, so an event's probability is its size divided by the sample space size.
Pr[A | B] = Pr[A ∩ B] / Pr[B]: the chance of A once you know B happened. B becomes the new sample space.
Pr[A ∩ B] = Pr[A | B] · Pr[B]. It is why you multiply probabilities along the edges of a tree diagram.
Pr[B | A] = Pr[A | B] · Pr[B] / Pr[A]. It reverses the direction of a conditional probability.
The prior is your belief before seeing evidence. The posterior is your updated belief after conditioning on that evidence.
Pr[A ∪ B] ≤ Pr[A] + Pr[B] for any events, because the overlap you skip subtracting is never negative.
A trend that holds within every group but reverses when the groups are combined, because the groups have different sizes or weights.
A and B are independent when Pr[A ∩ B] = Pr[A]·Pr[B]: learning one happened doesn't change the odds of the other.
Pr[A] = Pr[E]·Pr[A | E] + Pr[not E]·Pr[A | not E]. It is a proof by cases on any event E.
Every pair of events in a collection is independent. This is weaker than mutual independence.
Every sub-collection of the events satisfies the product rule, so you may multiply any group of their probabilities.
Among d equally likely values, a repeat becomes more likely than not after about 1.18√d random picks, such as 23 people for 365 days.
The false belief that independent trials balance out, for example that tails is 'due' after a run of heads.
A function from the sample space to the real numbers. It is neither random nor a variable: the randomness is in which outcome occurs.
An RV that only takes the values 0 and 1. It equals 1 exactly on the outcomes of some event A.
Pr[R₁ = x and R₂ = y] = Pr[R₁ = x]·Pr[R₂ = y] for every pair of values x and y.
Probability mass function: PMF(x) = Pr[R = x], the probability that the RV takes exactly the value x.
Cumulative distribution function: CDF(x) = Pr[R ≤ x], the running total of the PMF.
The number of heads in n independent coins with heads probability p. Pr[k] = C(n,k) p^k (1−p)^(n−k).
The probability-weighted average of a random variable's values; the long-run average if you repeat the experiment many times.
A random variable equal to 1 when an event happens and 0 otherwise. Its expectation equals the event's probability.
For a variable taking natural-number values, E[X] equals the sum over i ≥ 0 of Pr[X > i].
The expected number of independent trials until the first success, equal to 1/p when each trial succeeds with probability p.
The distribution of how many independent trials you wait until the first success.
E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] and E[cX] = cE[X], for any random variables, with no independence required.
The chance that at least one event happens is at most the sum of their probabilities. Always true, but useless once the sum exceeds 1.
For mutually independent events, the chance at least one happens is at least 1 − e^(−E[N]), where E[N] is the expected number of events.
If X and Y are independent, E[XY] = E[X]·E[Y]. It can fail when they are dependent.
Var[X] = E[(X − E[X])²]: the average squared distance from the mean. Equivalently E[X²] − E[X]².
The square root of the variance, measuring spread in the same units as the random variable itself.
Splitting an amount across k independent risks. The mean stays the same while variance drops by a factor of k.
An upper limit on the probability that a random variable lands far from its expected value.
If R is never negative, Pr[R ≥ x] ≤ E[R]/x. Needs only the mean.
Subtract a known lower limit before applying Markov. This makes it valid for variables that can be negative, or stronger when the minimum exceeds 0.
For any random variable, Pr[|R − E[R]| ≥ x] ≤ Var[R]/x². It comes from applying Markov to the squared deviation.
For a sum of mutually independent pieces each between 0 and 1, the chance of reaching c times the mean shrinks exponentially in the mean.
A bound that some distribution meets exactly, so it cannot be improved using only the same information.
